name: Skin cycling

image.caption: Cycling past Skinner's Lock, Grantham Canal - geograph.org.uk - 6452000

lead: Skin cycling rotates a four-night routine: a chemical exfoliant night, a retinoid night, then two nights with no actives. People use it for acne, scars, fine lines and glow, and it is promoted for sensitive or acne-prone skin.

The rest nights let the skin barrier recover between exfoliation and retinoid use, so irritation builds less than with daily actives and the skin builds tolerance. It was introduced by dermatologist Whitney Bowe in April 2021 and went viral on TikTok in 2022. No clinical study has tested this specific schedule; dermatologists quoted describe it as consistent with alternating strong actives with rest.

paras: The cycle repeats continuously. Mornings are the same every day, gentle cleansing and broad-spectrum sunscreen, and recovery nights use moisturising, barrier-supporting products. Retinoid results are generally described over weeks to months.
Exfoliants and retinoids can cause dryness, redness and sun sensitivity, so daily sunscreen is part of the method. It is not described as a replacement for professional treatment of severe acne.

angle.text: Rotating acid and retinoid nights with recovery nights lets you keep using actives for acne, scars, fine lines and glow with less irritation, which is what makes smoother, clearer skin sustainable. The schedule was popularised by a dermatologist and TikTok and has not itself been trialled.

lead: Skin cycling is a skincare routine that rotates evenings of active ingredients with evenings of recovery. It was introduced in April 2021 by New York dermatologist Whitney Bowe and spread widely on TikTok in 2022.[1]

The standard four-night cycle uses a chemical exfoliant on night one, a retinoid on night two, and no actives on nights three and four, when moisturising and barrier-supporting products are used instead. Mornings are the same each day: gentle cleansing and broad-spectrum sunscreen.[1] Proponents say it reduces irritation while building tolerance to retinoids and exfoliants.[1]

No published clinical studies have tested this specific schedule. Dermatologists quoted in general references describe it as a reasonable framework consistent with alternating strong actives with rest, while noting that retinoid data mostly support regular use.[1]

paras: Night one uses a chemical exfoliant such as an alpha or beta hydroxy acid; physical scrubs are discouraged in the description of the method. Night two uses a retinoid, either over-the-counter retinol or prescription tretinoin, applied in a small amount. Nights three and four contain no actives and focus on hydration and barrier repair with ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides and niacinamide.[1]

Daytime routine is constant: gentle cleansing, optional moisturiser and broad-spectrum sunscreen of at least SPF 30, because exfoliants and retinoids increase sun sensitivity.[1] Variants exist with more recovery nights for sensitive skin and fewer for experienced users.[1]
The method was introduced by Whitney Bowe in April 2021 and gained mass attention on TikTok in 2022, with the hashtag drawing billions of views.[1]

No published clinical studies have tested this regimen. Dermatologists generally describe the approach as reasonable, since it follows the established practice of pairing potent actives with rest, though retinoid evidence mainly supports regular use for best results.[1] Over-exfoliation is described in general references as able to irritate skin and damage its barrier.[2]

Noted limitations include slower visible results for people whose skin tolerates daily actives, the discipline required, changes that can take eight weeks or longer, and that it does not replace professional treatment for conditions such as cystic acne or melasma.[1]

lore.intro: Skin cycling is discussed in skincare and looksmaxxing communities as a way to use retinoids and acids without a damaged skin barrier.[1]

claims.claim: Alternating actives with rest nights gives retinoid results with less irritation.
Skin cycling suits sensitive, acne-prone or barrier-damaged skin.

timeline.event: Dermatologist Whitney Bowe introduces skin cycling in April.[1]
The routine spreads widely through TikTok.[1]
